prompt.context: Our client is Ducati, a leading Italian producer of motorcycles. They produce high-end motorbikes which they sell globally. They have 150 stores: 50 stores are single-brand (they only sell Ducati) and the remaining 100 stores are multi-brand (they sell between 3 and 8 different brands of motorbikes). Multi-brand stores have similar sales and income figures, while single-brand stores are either huge successes or on the verge of bankruptcy.
prompt.question: Ducati hired ADL because they want to identify the major reasons for this disparity between single-brand and multi-brand store performance, and find a way to decrease the number of underperforming single-brand stores. How would you structure this problem, and what recommendation would you give to the CEO?

clarifying_info.q: Is the distribution of underperforming single-brand stores concentrated in particular geographies (urban/suburban, EU/USA/Asia)?
clarifying_info.a: The distribution of underperforming single-brand stores is uniform among cities, suburban areas, and different countries.

clarifying_info.q: Has Ducati done a customer segmentation analysis for each area where single-brand stores are placed?
clarifying_info.a: Ducati has a clear value proposition and the customer analysis is well structured.

clarifying_info.q: Does Ducati treat single-brand and multi-brand store managers differently?
clarifying_info.a: Ducati treats MB and SB store managers in the same way. Once a new store manager decides to open a new store, they ask Ducati to supply motorbikes; Ducati decides to accept or not based on strategic/location factors. No further consideration is made based on SB vs MB nature.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any geographic correlation between the distribution of performing single-brand stores and multi-brand stores or competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The best single-brand stores are localized close to competitors or multi-brand stores. The bigger the multi-brand store, the higher the performance of the nearby single-brand store.

framework: Geography: Examine whether underperforming SB stores are concentrated in particular areas (urban/suburban) or countries (EU/USA/Asia)
Customers: Assess whether Ducati targeted the right customer segments in each area where an SB store was positioned
Store management: Evaluate whether Ducati’s relationship with SB managers differs from MB managers (incentives, support, training)
Store-level differences: Analyze client mix and traffic differences between SB and MB stores — size, customer type, foot traffic, cross-selling exposure
Brand recognition: Determine whether potential loyal customers in a given region are aware of the Ducati riding experience
Cross-selling / traffic spillover: Identify whether proximity to competitor or MB stores drives traffic and brand discovery for SB stores

questions.prompt: What are the major structural differences between single-brand and multi-brand stores?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers: (1) Size — SB stores tend to be smaller than MB. (2) Customer profile — SB attracts mostly Ducati enthusiasts or curious customers; MB attracts all motorbike shoppers. (3) Manager profile — SB manager is likely a Ducati enthusiast but not necessarily an experienced seller; MB manager is likely an experienced retail operator. (4) Traffic — MB stores attract far more customers; the more brands carried, the higher the foot traffic.

questions.prompt: Evidence shows that SB stores with higher traffic are more likely to perform better. What are the possible reasons for this traffic-performance correlation?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies brand recognition as the core mechanism: in many markets Ducati has not yet established customer captivity (e.g., in the US there is no equivalent of Harley-Davidson brand loyalty for Ducati yet). Potential loyal customers may simply have never encountered a Ducati. Higher-traffic environments expose more prospective buyers to the brand, converting curious visitors into loyal ‘Ducatisti’.

questions.prompt: How would you identify indicators of SB store traffic potential without physically visiting each store?
questions.guidance: Look for proximity to competitor stores and/or multi-brand stores — especially large MB stores carrying 7–8 brands. These act as traffic generators. Indicators: density of competitor/MB stores within a radius, market enthusiasm for motorbikes in the region, presence of large MB anchors nearby. Data shows best SB stores are co-located with competitors or MB stores, and performance correlates positively with MB store size.

brainstorming.prompt: What can Ducati infer from the finding that the best SB stores are located near competitors or large multi-brand stores?

categories.name: Cross-selling effect
ideas: MB stores expose non-Ducati shoppers to the brand while they browse other bikes
Customers who discover Ducati at a MB store may later become loyal SB customers
Larger MB stores with 7–8 brands generate higher foot traffic, amplifying brand exposure

categories.name: Brand recognition / captivity
ideas: Ducati lacks customer captivity in most markets (unlike Harley-Davidson in the US)
Regions with dense competitor/MB store presence have higher baseline motorbike interest and awareness
Proximity to rivals normalizes the category purchase and makes Ducati more discoverable

categories.name: Location strategy implications
ideas: New SB stores should be sited near existing MB clusters or competitor stores
Showrooms in high-MB-density zones can leverage pre-built category traffic
Ducati should map MB store density before committing to new SB locations

recommendation: Ducati should map all areas with high concentrations of multi-brand and competitor stores, as these zones generate the foot traffic and brand exposure that underpin SB store success
Invest in opening new single-brand stores and showrooms in these high-density zones to leverage the brand recognition and cross-selling traffic already created by MB stores
Avoid opening isolated SB stores in areas without nearby MB or competitor presence until Ducati brand recognition reaches sufficient depth in that market
risks: Cannibalization risk if SB store is positioned too close to an MB store that already sells Ducati
Real-estate and build-out costs in high-traffic commercial zones may be substantially higher
Brand recognition alone may not be sufficient if SB store management quality is weak — manager training and support should accompany the location strategy
recommendation.risks_note: Secondary risks include real-estate costs and management quality
next_steps: Conduct a systematic geo-mapping exercise: overlay SB store performance data with MB store locations and density
Develop a location scoring model incorporating MB store density, competitor proximity, and regional motorbike enthusiasm
Pilot 2–3 new SB stores or showrooms in high-scoring zones and track conversion and sales lift
Assess whether SB store manager training and operational support should be upgraded in parallel
